routeb.note: Trace: one node's share (1/24, sessions kept together) of 2026-09-18 11:05–11:15 UTC, 727 requests, engines started cold. The DSpark engine's 106 s TTFT is queueing: its max running requests is 128 (the CUDA-graph envelope) and cold prefills of 50–650k prompts in 8k chunks stall decode across the DP lockstep, so slots are held for minutes and arrivals wait. Production sees 98.9% cache hits because sessions continue; a cold replay does not. The staircase warms the caches with the preceding 30 minutes first, which is the fair measurement.

summary: Where we are, in one breath: the vendor's demo as shipped did 0.72 M TPM per GPU. Two fixes (a Triton recompile patch and 8 tokenizer workers) and one swap (the older engine build that keeps DSpark on CUDA graphs) took the node to 3.20 M per GPU on the manual's static frame; the production-shaped 4×tp2 layout under a KV router nudged that to 3.34 M (48% of the north star) and decodes 2.8× faster per stream on real traffic. On real traffic both layouts still knee at about 2.5 req/s (≈ 1 M per GPU sustained) because cold prefill dominates: the single engine keeps 91% cache hits, the 4-worker layout only 60%. Routing affinity is the next lever.

metrics: Real-traffic capacity at production-parity latency: the highest staircase level whose per-minute TTFT p50 ≤ 1.6 s and p99 ≤ 22 s, replaying a node's share of the real peak hour after a cache warm-up. Reported in req/s per node and TPM per GPU. This answers whether the node can take production traffic, and how much.

Static frame: 80k cached prefix / 128 new / 600 output, the M3 manual's TPM test and the kind of figure behind the 7 M/GPU claim. Random-token text, so spec decode gains do not show; one shared prefix, so affinity routing must not be used.

The static test rewards raw concurrency with a load-balanced router; real traffic rewards cache affinity and low prefill stall. The same 4×tp2 layout wins both once the router matches the test; production's strict-affinity policy (affinity only on high overlap, else load) serves both at once.

tests.note: Yes, they differ a lot: the same node shows 3.2–3.7 M/GPU on the static frame and 1–1.5 M/GPU sustained on real traffic. The gap is not error: static requests are 100% cached and identical, while real requests carry 5–60k uncached tokens each (9–12% of 50–650k prompts), and that prefill is most of the GPU time. The static frame also hides spec decode and routing effects, and the replay can rank layouts in the opposite order (tp8 vs 4×tp2 are equal on static, but only 4×tp2 + affinity holds 4× load on real traffic). The closed-loop replay isolates the prompt-mix effect (same load control as static, real prompts), so the three together separate 'prompt mix' from 'arrival pattern'.
